categories.name: Information Gathering
categories.description: Passive/active information gathering, discovery and mapping work about the target application and infrastructure.

tests.title: Search Engine Discovery (Google Dorking)
tests.description: Detect leaked information, directory listings and sensitive files related to the target via search engines and cache records.
steps: Scan the target domain using Google/Bing dork operators (site:, filetype:, intitle:).
Review deleted/old pages through Wayback Machine and Google Cache.
Search for leaked keys/passwords on sources such as GitHub and Pastebin.
Report the information found (email, server path, version info).
tests.example: site:target.com filetype:sql OR filetype:env OR intitle:"index of"

tests.title: Web Server Fingerprinting
tests.description: Determine the server software and version from HTTP headers and behavioral differences.
steps: Inspect the Server and X-Powered-By headers.
Send a malformed request and analyze the error page format.
Gather server info via banner grabbing during a port scan.
Confirm your findings with active scanning tools.

tests.title: Review Web Server Metafiles
tests.description: Discover paths that are being hidden through files such as robots.txt, sitemap.xml, and security.txt.
steps: Fetch the /robots.txt and /sitemap.xml files.
Manually visit the disallowed paths.
Check for humans.txt, security.txt and .well-known/ directories.
Test the discovered paths for accessibility.

tests.title: Enumerate Applications on the Server
tests.description: Discover other applications and subdomains hosted on the same server/IP.
steps: Run virtual host (vhost) and subdomain enumeration tools.
Find other sites on the same IP with a reverse IP lookup.
Extract subdomain information from SSL certificate SAN fields.
Document the access and purpose of the applications found.

tests.title: Review Webpage Content
tests.description: Look for sensitive data leakage in HTML/JS source code, comments, and hidden form fields.
steps: Inspect the page source code and comment lines.
Download JS files and search for API keys/endpoints.
Check hidden input fields and meta tags.
Record developer notes and TODO comments.

tests.title: Identify Application Entry Points
tests.description: Map every parameter, form and endpoint that accepts user input.
steps: Browse the application through a proxy and log every request.
List GET/POST parameters, headers and cookies.
Flag entry points inside multi-step flows (checkout, registration).
Catalog every entry point for use in later tests.
tests.example: Burp Suite Target > Site Map to list all parameters

tests.title: Map Execution Paths Through the Application
tests.description: Expand test coverage by mapping workflows and possible code paths within the application.
steps: Automatically crawl every page with a spider/crawler.
Manually test the different flows per user role (admin/user).
Document the order of multi-step processes (payment, approval).
Correlate the resulting site map with the other test steps.

tests.title: Fingerprint Web Application Framework
tests.description: Detect the backend framework in use (Laravel, Django, Express, etc.).
steps: Look for framework signatures in HTTP headers (X-Powered-By, cookie name).
Trigger the framework-specific error page format.
Check the framework-specific directory structure in static file paths.
Research known CVEs for the detected framework.

tests.title: Fingerprint Web Application
tests.description: Determine the type and version of the CMS, e-commerce platform, or custom-built application.
steps: Check the meta generator tag and static file paths (wp-content, /sites/all).
Confirm the version from changelog or README files.
Test CMS-specific admin login paths (/wp-admin, /administrator).
Search a CVE database for known flaws in the version found.

tests.title: Map Application Architecture
tests.description: Extract the application's components (CDN, load balancer, API gateway, database layer) and data flow.
steps: Identify infrastructure components from DNS records (CNAME, MX, TXT).
Detect the presence of a CDN/WAF from response headers and IP ranges.
Gather traces of a microservice architecture from API calls.
Document the resulting architecture with a diagram.

categories.name: Configuration and Deployment Management Testing
categories.description: Test for misconfigurations in the server, application platform and deployment processes.

tests.title: Test Network Infrastructure Configuration
tests.description: Detect open ports, unnecessary services and network-level misconfigurations.
steps: Run a port scan across the target IP range.
Assess whether services on open ports are actually necessary.
Check whether management interfaces (SSH, RDP, database ports) are exposed externally.
Report that unnecessary services should be disabled.

tests.title: Test Application Platform Configuration
tests.description: Test the web/application server for default settings and leftover sample files.
steps: Check default installation pages (/phpinfo.php, /server-status).
Test the accessibility of admin consoles (Tomcat Manager, phpMyAdmin).
Check whether directory listing is enabled.
Inspect the verbosity of error messages (stack trace, version).

tests.title: Test File Extensions Handling for Sensitive Information
tests.description: Test whether backup/source code extensions (.bak, .old, .zip) are served by the server without being executed.
steps: Try common backup extensions appended to known file names.
Run an automated scan with extension fuzzing.
Check whether version-control directories such as .git and .svn are exposed.
Inspect any source code/credentials found in discovered files.

tests.title: Review Old Backup and Unreferenced Files
tests.description: Find old/test files that remain on the server but are no longer linked from the application.
steps: Try common file names (test.php, backup.zip) with directory fuzzing.
Search the Wayback Machine for old pages that no longer have live links.
Follow references to old files left in comments.
Review the content of discovered files for sensitive data.

tests.title: Enumerate Infrastructure and Application Admin Interfaces
tests.description: Test the existence and access control of administrative panels.
steps: Run directory fuzzing with a common admin path list (/admin, /manage, /cpanel).
Try default credentials on any panels found.
Check whether panel access is restricted by IP.
Document the impact if unauthorized access is possible.

tests.title: Test HTTP Methods
tests.description: Test whether dangerous or unnecessary HTTP methods (PUT, DELETE, TRACE) are enabled.
steps: Send an OPTIONS request to list the supported methods.
Try uploading/deleting a file using PUT/DELETE.
Check for Cross-Site Tracing (XST) potential via the TRACE method.
Test whether WebDAV methods (PROPFIND) are enabled.

tests.title: Test HTTP Strict Transport Security
tests.description: Check for the presence and correct configuration of the HSTS header.
steps: Check the response header for the Strict-Transport-Security field.
Confirm the max-age value is sufficiently long.
Check the use of the includeSubDomains and preload directives.
Test whether HTTP is automatically redirected to HTTPS.

tests.title: Test RIA Cross Domain Policy
tests.description: Test whether crossdomain.xml and clientaccesspolicy.xml files are overly permissive.
steps: Fetch the /crossdomain.xml and /clientaccesspolicy.xml files.
Look for overly permissive rules such as allow-access-from domain="*".
Assess whether the allowed domains are actually trustworthy.
Correlate the findings with the CORS tests.

tests.title: Test File Permissions
tests.description: Test whether file and directory permissions on the server are overly broad.
steps: Check the read/write permissions of accessible files (with server access if possible).
Test whether uploaded files are saved with executable permissions.
Review the permissions of backup scripts.
Report any overly permissive files.

tests.title: Test for Subdomain Takeover
tests.description: Detect subdomains that have a DNS record but point to cloud services that are no longer in use.
steps: List all subdomains along with their CNAME records.
Check whether the CNAME target (S3, GitHub Pages, Heroku, etc.) is still active.
Confirm dangling CNAMEs using automated tools.
Document the impact (phishing, cookie theft) if takeover is possible.

tests.title: Test Cloud Storage
tests.description: Test for misconfigured permissions on cloud storage such as S3 buckets and Azure Blob.
steps: Identify bucket names from application source code and DNS.
Check whether the bucket is publicly listable.
Test whether write access is possible (try uploading a file).
Document whether sensitive files are publicly accessible.

categories.name: Identity Management Testing
categories.description: Test security weaknesses in role definitions, registration and account-provisioning processes.

tests.title: Test Role Definitions
tests.description: Assess whether the roles in the application (admin, editor, user) are clearly separated.
steps: List every role in the application and its permissions.
Check for overlapping permissions between roles.
Compare the role matrix against real access tests.
Report any overly privileged role definitions.
tests.example: Build an access matrix for each role and test every endpoint

tests.title: Test User Registration Process
tests.description: Test the validation and abuse-prevention mechanisms in the registration form.
steps: Check whether email verification can be skipped.
Test whether duplicate registration with the same details is prevented.
Try manipulating a role/permission parameter in the registration form (mass assignment).
Test for the presence of a CAPTCHA/rate limit.

tests.title: Test Account Provisioning Process
tests.description: Test whether the account creation/deletion process is protected against unauthorized use.
steps: Test whether it's possible to create an account on behalf of another user.
Check that provisioning APIs require authentication.
Confirm that deleted accounts are actually deactivated.
Test whether approval steps in the process can be skipped.
tests.example: Send a request to the provisioning endpoint with an unauthorized user

tests.title: Testing for Account Enumeration and Guessable User Account
tests.description: Test whether login/registration/password-reset forms leak the existence of a user.
steps: Compare error messages between login attempts with existing and non-existing usernames.
Measure differences in response times (timing).
Repeat the same test on the password reset form.
Check for differences in HTTP status code/response size.
tests.example: POST /login user=admin  vs  user=random123  -> difference in error message

tests.title: Testing for Weak or Unenforced Username Policy
tests.description: Test the predictability of username-generation rules.
steps: Check whether usernames are email addresses or sequential IDs.
Test whether the username format follows a predictable pattern.
Assess whether a list of usernames can be derived.
Correlate the findings with the account enumeration test.
tests.example: Scan sequential IDs such as user1, user2, user3 ...

categories.name: Authentication Testing
categories.description: Test login mechanisms, password policies and authentication bypass methods.

tests.title: Testing for Credentials Transported over an Encrypted Channel
tests.description: Test whether the username/password is sent over an unencrypted (HTTP) channel.
steps: Confirm the login form is served over HTTPS.
Check that the form action does not fall back to HTTP.
Review mixed-content warnings (HTTP resource on an HTTPS page).
Capture the traffic with a proxy and confirm the encryption status.
tests.example: Capture traffic with Burp Suite and check the protocol of the login request

tests.title: Testing for Default Credentials
tests.description: Test whether default/guessable credentials remain in place on the application or its components.
steps: Try the known default username/password list for the product/framework (admin/admin).
Test default credentials on admin panels.
Check default access credentials on IoT/CMS components.
Recommend changing any default accounts found.
tests.example: Try combinations such as admin:admin, admin:password, root:root

tests.title: Testing for Weak Lock Out Mechanism
tests.description: Test the effectiveness of the lockout/rate-limit mechanism against failed login attempts.
steps: Try many wrong passwords in a row and observe the lockout threshold.
Determine whether the lockout is IP-based or account-based.
Try lockout bypass methods (changing X-Forwarded-For).
Assess whether the lockout duration is reasonable.
tests.example: Send 50+ attempts with Burp Intruder and observe the lockout behavior

tests.title: Testing for Bypassing Authentication Schema
tests.description: Test whether the login step can be skipped via direct URL access, parameter manipulation, or similar methods.
steps: Try accessing post-login pages directly via URL.
Manipulate token/parameter values (isAdmin=true, auth=1).
Look for unprotected endpoints via force browsing.
Try bypassing client-side controls (JS-based redirection).
tests.example: Call GET /dashboard directly (without a session) and check the response

tests.title: Testing for Vulnerable Remember Password
tests.description: Test the token security and predictability of the remember-me function.
steps: Decode the content of the remember-me cookie/token.
Check whether the token follows a predictable pattern.
Test whether the token is invalidated on a password change.
Assess whether the token is unlimited/long-lived.

tests.title: Testing for Browser Cache Weaknesses
tests.description: Test whether sensitive pages remain in the browser cache or are reachable via the back button.
steps: Check that Cache-Control and Pragma headers are set on sensitive pages.
Test access to the page via the back button after logging out.
Check whether sensitive data remains in the browser's disk cache.
Review autocomplete settings for forms.

tests.title: Testing for Weak Password Policy
tests.description: Test the adequacy of password complexity and length requirements.
steps: Test the minimum length and character variety requirements.
Try whether common/weak passwords (123456, password) are accepted.
Test whether password history (reuse of an old password) is checked.
Confirm the policy is enforced server-side, not just client-side.
tests.example: Try registering/changing a password with weak values such as "123456", "password", "qwerty"

tests.title: Testing for Weak Security Question Answer
tests.description: Test the predictability of the security questions used for password recovery.
steps: Assess whether the offered security questions are easily researchable.
Check whether the answer format is restricted/predictable.
Test whether there is a retry limit for the same question.
Assess whether the answer can be discovered via OSINT.
tests.example: Look for questions discoverable via OSINT, such as "What is your first pet's name?"

tests.title: Testing for Weak Password Change or Reset Functionalities
tests.description: Test the token security and possible unauthorized use of the password reset flow.
steps: Test whether the reset token is predictable/reusable.
Check whether the token's lifetime is reasonable.
Test whether a change is allowed without verifying the old password.
Check whether the token leaks in the URL (Referer header).
tests.example: Decode the token in the reset link and test its predictability

tests.title: Testing for Weaker Authentication in Alternative Channel
tests.description: Test whether alternative access channels, such as a mobile API or an old API version, contain weaker authentication.
steps: Route mobile app/API traffic through a proxy and review authentication differences.
Check whether old API versions are still reachable.
Confirm the alternative channel enforces the same security level as the main channel.
Report inconsistencies across different channels.
tests.example: Run the mobile app through the Burp proxy and inspect /api/v1 endpoints

categories.name: Authorization Testing
categories.description: Test access control, permission boundaries and object-level authorization flaws.

tests.title: Testing Directory Traversal File Include
tests.description: Test whether unauthorized files can be accessed via path traversal.
steps: Inject ../ sequences into parameters that accept a file path.
Try URL-encoded and double-encoded variations.
Test different path traversal sequences for Windows/Linux.
Confirm the content of the accessed file (/etc/passwd, web.config).

tests.title: Testing for Bypassing Authorization Schema
tests.description: Test whether access control rules can be bypassed via parameter/path manipulation.
steps: Try accessing protected endpoints with different HTTP methods (POST instead of GET).
Try normalization differences in the URL, such as case changes or extra slashes.
Bypass client-side controls (a menu hidden with JS) to reach the endpoint directly.
Test for inconsistencies between API versions (v1 protected, v2 unprotected).

tests.title: Testing for Privilege Escalation
tests.description: Test whether a low-privileged user can reach higher-privileged functionality (horizontal/vertical privilege escalation).
steps: Call high-privilege endpoints directly with a low-privilege account.
Manipulate role/permission parameters (role=admin, isAdmin=true).
Test access to another user's data at the same privilege level (horizontal escalation).
Try modifying the permission claims inside a JWT/token.

tests.title: Testing for Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR)
tests.description: Test whether object IDs (user, order, file) can be modified without authorization checks.
steps: Note the ID of your own resource and capture the request.
Increment/decrement the ID value or swap it for another user's ID.
Check whether sequential, predictable IDs are used.
Test whether unauthorized access to other resources is possible even when UUIDs are used.
tests.example:
GET /api/orders/1042 -> your own order
GET /api/orders/1043 -> another user's order (unauthorized access)

categories.name: Session Management Testing
categories.description: Test security weaknesses in the generation, transport and termination of session tokens.

tests.title: Testing for Session Management Schema
tests.description: Test the randomness and predictability of the session ID generation algorithm.
steps: Collect multiple session IDs and run an entropy analysis.
Check whether IDs contain a timestamp or a sequential pattern.
Check whether the session ID is carried in the URL (risk of leaking into logs).
Test whether a repeated ID is ever generated for the same user.
tests.example: Collect 100+ session tokens with Burp Sequencer and measure entropy

tests.title: Testing for Cookies Attributes
tests.description: Test whether session cookies are protected by the HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite flags.
steps: Check the Set-Cookie header for the HttpOnly flag.
Confirm the Secure flag is set in an HTTPS context.
Assess whether the SameSite value (Strict/Lax) is sufficient CSRF protection.
Test whether the cookie is readable via JS through document.cookie.
tests.example:
curl -I https://target.com | grep -i set-cookie
# Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Strict expected

tests.title: Testing for Session Fixation
tests.description: Test whether a session ID known before login remains valid after login.
steps: Obtain a session ID before authentication (or set one yourself).
Log in with that ID and check whether it changes after login.
If it doesn't change, simulate injecting the ID into a victim and hijacking the session.
Confirm the server issues a new ID on every authentication.
tests.example: Fix the cookie before login: Cookie: session=ABC123 -> check whether it's the same after login

tests.title: Testing for Exposed Session Variables
tests.description: Test whether session information leaks via the URL, logs, or the Referer header.
steps: Check whether the session ID is carried as a URL parameter.
Test whether the token leaks in the Referer header sent to external links.
Check whether the session ID is logged in plaintext in server/proxy logs.
Assess whether a sensitive token remains in the browser history.
tests.example: GET /page?PHPSESSID=abc123 -> carrying a token in the URL is risky

tests.title: Testing for Cross Site Request Forgery (CSRF)
tests.description: Test whether critical actions can be triggered from third-party sites without CSRF token validation.
steps: Capture a request for a critical action, strip the CSRF token field, and resend it.
Replace the token with an invalid value and check whether the server rejects it.
Assess whether the SameSite cookie setting prevents CSRF.
Build a proof-of-concept HTML page with an auto-submitting form and test it.
tests.example:
<form action="https://target.com/transfer" method="POST">
<input name="to" value="attacker"><input name="amount" value="1000">
</form><script>document.forms[0].submit()</script>

tests.title: Testing for Logout Functionality
tests.description: Test that the logout process fully invalidates the session on the server side.
steps: Log out and resend the old request using the old session ID.
Confirm logout happens on both the client (cookie removal) and server (session invalidation) sides.
Test that all sessions end in a multi-device/multi-tab scenario.
Try accessing a protected page again after logout.
tests.example: Send a GET /dashboard request with the old Cookie header after logout

tests.title: Testing Session Timeout
tests.description: Test that idle sessions are terminated within a reasonable time.
steps: Log in and remain idle for an extended period.
Check at intervals whether the session is still valid.
Test the absolute timeout and the idle timeout separately.
Assess whether the timeout duration is reasonable for the application's sensitivity.
tests.example: Capture a session token and reuse it in a request 30/60/120 minutes later

tests.title: Testing for Session Puzzling
tests.description: Test whether session variables are unexpectedly reused across different functions.
steps: Map the variables (state, step) the application keeps in the session.
Test whether a session variable set in one function affects another function.
Try skipping a step in a multi-step process to manipulate the session state.
Check whether unexpected state transitions lead to authorization bypass.
tests.example: Try triggering the 'verified' session variable from the password-reset flow in a different flow

tests.title: Testing for Session Hijacking
tests.description: Test whether a session token can be stolen over the network or via XSS.
steps: Confirm the traffic is HTTPS-encrypted and the token is never exposed.
If an XSS flaw exists, test whether the token can be stolen via document.cookie.
Test whether a stolen token can be used from a different device/IP (session binding).
Check whether the token is bound to an IP/User-Agent.

categories.name: Input Validation Testing
categories.description: Test the injection flaws that arise when user input is not adequately validated.

tests.title: Reflected Cross Site Scripting (XSS)
tests.description: Test for cases where user input is reflected directly into the page and can execute a script.
steps: Send a test payload to every entry point (parameter, header).
Identify where the payload is reflected in the response without being encoded.
Adapt the payload to different contexts (HTML, attribute, JS).
If a WAF/filter is present, try bypass variations.

tests.title: Stored Cross Site Scripting (XSS)
tests.description: Test for cases where user input is stored in a database and executes a script when served to other users.
steps: Send the payload to persistent data fields such as comments, profiles or messages.
Check whether the payload executes when viewed by another user/page.
If a rich text editor is present, try bypassing the HTML whitelist.
Demonstrate the impact (cookie theft, admin panel takeover) with a PoC.
tests.example: In the profile bio field:

tests.title: HTTP Verb Tampering
tests.description: Test whether the application handles different HTTP methods inconsistently, bypassing access control.
steps: Send requests to a protected endpoint with methods such as HEAD, PUT or DELETE instead of GET.
Test whether the permission check is only enforced for certain methods.
Observe whether the method change triggers a different code path.
Report any inconsistencies found.
tests.example: DELETE /admin/users/5  (GET may be protected while DELETE is not)

tests.title: HTTP Parameter Pollution
tests.description: Test the inconsistent behavior of the application/WAF when the same parameter is sent multiple times.
steps: Send the same parameter multiple times with different values.
Determine whether the backend processes the first or the last value.
Try using parameter repetition to bypass a WAF/filter.
Detect processing differences between layers (WAF, application server).

tests.title: SQL Injection
tests.description: Test for cases where user input is inserted directly into database queries and can alter the query logic (MySQL, MSSQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, NoSQL).
steps: Try triggering an error with a single/double quote and comment characters (--, #).
Confirm with boolean-based and time-based blind techniques.
Try exfiltrating data with UNION SELECT.
Use database-specific syntax (MySQL: SLEEP(), MSSQL: WAITFOR, Oracle: DBMS_LOCK); for NoSQL try the $where/$ne operators.
tests.example:
' OR '1'='1' -- 
' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- 
'; WAITFOR DELAY '0:0:5'--

tests.title: LDAP Injection
tests.description: Test whether special characters injected into LDAP queries can alter the filter logic.
steps: Send LDAP special characters (*, (, ), \) into input fields.
Try bypassing the authentication filter.
Try exfiltrating data with a wildcard (blind LDAP injection).
Gather information about the LDAP structure from error messages.

tests.title: XML Injection
tests.description: Test whether the XML parser is vulnerable to external entity (XXE) or structure manipulation.
steps: Define an external entity via DOCTYPE in endpoints that accept XML.
Try file-read (file://) and SSRF (http://) scenarios.
Use out-of-band (OOB) techniques for blind XXE.
Confirm whether the parser disables DTD/external entity processing.

tests.title: SSI Injection
tests.description: Test whether server-side include (SSI) directives can be injected via user input.
steps: Send SSI directive syntax into input fields.
Check whether the server uses SSI-supporting extensions such as .shtml.
Try an RCE attempt with the exec cmd directive.
Confirm the directive was processed in the response (file content/command output).

tests.title: XPath Injection
tests.description: Test whether XPath queries can be manipulated via user input.
steps: Try triggering an error with a single quote.
Try bypassing authentication with boolean conditions (or 1=1).
Try character-by-character data extraction for blind XPath injection.
Gather information about the XML structure from error messages.

tests.title: IMAP/SMTP Injection
tests.description: Test whether IMAP/SMTP commands injected into email functions (contact form, search) can be executed.
steps: Try CRLF and command injection in an email field.
Try adding an extra recipient via BCC/header injection.
Test IMAP command injection in a mail search function.
Confirm whether the server interprets the input as a header.

tests.title: Local File Inclusion (LFI)
tests.description: Test whether local files on the server can be included and read via a file-path parameter.
steps: Send path traversal sequences to parameters that include a file.
Try reading source code with PHP wrappers (php://filter).
Try turning LFI into RCE via log poisoning.
Test null-byte or path-truncation bypass techniques on legacy systems.

tests.title: Remote File Inclusion (RFI)
tests.description: Test whether malicious code can be executed from a remote server via a file-include parameter.
steps: Point the include parameter to a URL on your own server.
Indirectly test whether settings such as allow_url_include are enabled.
Confirm whether the remote file is executed server-side (code output).
If RCE is achieved, document the impact in a controlled manner.

tests.title: Command Injection
tests.description: Test whether user input can be appended directly to an OS command and executed.
steps: Add command-separator characters (;, |, &&, $()) into input fields.
Confirm blind command injection with a time-based technique (sleep/ping).
Try executing a command directly where the output is visible in the response.
Try exfiltrating results using out-of-band (OOB) techniques.

tests.title: Format String Injection
tests.description: Test for printf-style format-string injection in C/C++-based applications.
steps: Send format specifiers such as %s, %x, %n into input fields.
Observe whether it causes the application to crash or leak memory.
Try gathering information via memory-address leaks (%x %x %x).
Assess the memory-write potential with %n (high risk, test carefully).

tests.title: Incubated Vulnerability Testing
tests.description: Test multi-stage flaws where malicious data is stored at one point and triggered at another point/time.
steps: Look for scenarios combining file upload with another function that processes that file.
Test whether stored XSS triggers in a different context, such as an admin panel.
Identify time-delayed triggers (scheduled tasks, batch jobs).
Confirm the multi-step attack chain end to end.
tests.example: Upload a malicious file name and wait for it to later be processed by a reporting engine

tests.title: HTTP Splitting/Smuggling
tests.description: Test whether HTTP response/request parsing can be manipulated via CRLF injection.
steps: Inject CRLF (%0d%0a) into parameters that populate a header value.
Try injecting extra headers/pages via response splitting.
Test a request-smuggling scenario using Content-Length inconsistencies (CL.TE / TE.CL).
Detect the parsing difference between the front end (proxy/CDN) and the back end.

tests.title: HTTP Incoming Requests Testing
tests.description: Test how the server handles abnormal/malformed HTTP requests.
steps: Send requests with missing/malformed headers.
Test server behavior with an oversized header or body.
Send a request with an unsupported HTTP version.
Check whether the server's error handling leaks information.

tests.title: Host Header Injection
tests.description: Test the flaw where the application trusts the Host header when building a redirect/link.
steps: Replace the Host header with a different domain.
Test whether the link in a password-reset email reflects the spoofed host.
Repeat the same test with the X-Forwarded-Host header.
Assess the potential for cache poisoning.

tests.title: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI)
tests.description: Test whether user input injected into a template engine (Jinja2, Twig, FreeMarker, etc.) executes code server-side.
steps: Send a template expression (${7*7}, {{7*7}}) and check whether it's processed.
If the computed value (49) appears in the response, identify the engine in use.
Try executing a command with an engine-specific RCE payload.
Confirm the impact (file read, command execution) in a controlled manner.

tests.title: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
tests.description: Test whether the server can be forced to request a user-controlled URL, reaching internal networks/services.
steps: Send an internal IP (127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254) to parameters that accept a URL.
Try accessing the cloud metadata endpoint (AWS/GCP/Azure).
Try bypassing filters with different protocols (file://, gopher://, dict://).
For blind SSRF, trigger a request to your own server (Burp Collaborator) and confirm.

categories.name: Error Handling Testing
categories.description: Test whether error messages leak excessive information.

tests.title: Testing for Improper Error Handling
tests.description: Test that the application does not show end users excessive technical detail in error states.
steps: Trigger errors with unexpected input (special characters, wrong type).
Check whether the error page contains version/path/query information.
Confirm status codes such as 404/500 return a customized page.
Test that API error responses are equally well controlled.
tests.example: GET /api/user?id=abc  (send a string where a number is expected)

tests.title: Testing for Stack Traces
tests.description: Test whether application errors are returned to the user along with a stack trace/debug information.
steps: Send requests that trigger errors and look for file paths/line numbers in the response.
Check whether framework-specific debug mode (e.g. Django DEBUG=True) is left on.
Record any library/version information leaked in a stack trace.
Correlate the findings with known CVEs.
tests.example: POST /api/process  body: malformed-json  -> look for a traceback in the response

categories.name: Weak Cryptography Testing
categories.description: Test whether encryption protocols and algorithms are current and secure.

tests.title: Testing for Weak Transport Layer Security
tests.description: Test that the TLS configuration uses up-to-date cipher suites and disables weak protocols.
steps: Scan the supported SSL/TLS versions (confirm SSLv3, TLS1.0 are disabled).
Check for the use of weak/deprecated cipher suites.
Validate the certificate and its chain.
Test for known TLS flaws (Heartbleed, POODLE).

tests.title: Testing for Padding Oracle
tests.description: Test whether data encrypted in CBC mode leaks information through padding errors.
steps: Modify bytes in an encrypted cookie/parameter and observe error-message differences.
Check whether there's a response difference between padding errors and other error types.
Attempt decrypt/encrypt with an automated padding-oracle tool.
If a flaw exists, demonstrate the impact (data decryption) with a PoC.

tests.title: Testing for Sensitive Information Sent via Unencrypted Channels
tests.description: Test whether sensitive data (password, credit card, personal information) is transmitted over HTTP or otherwise unencrypted.
steps: Confirm every request containing sensitive data uses HTTPS.
Check for mixed-content warnings.
Check whether API responses return more sensitive data than necessary (full credit card number).
Repeat the same test on mobile app traffic.
tests.example: Monitor traffic with Burp Suite and look for sensitive fields sent over HTTP

tests.title: Testing for Weak Encryption
tests.description: Test whether the application uses weak or crackable algorithms such as MD5/SHA1.
steps: Guess the algorithm from the password hash format (length, prefix).
Check whether a salt is used.
If a weak algorithm is found, attempt hash cracking.
Recommend migrating to modern algorithms such as bcrypt/scrypt/Argon2.
tests.example: hashcat -m 0 hash.txt rockyou.txt  # if MD5 is detected

categories.name: Business Logic Testing
categories.description: Test logical flaws that are technically valid requests but bypass business rules.

tests.title: Test Business Logic Data Validation
tests.description: Test whether the application accepts data that violates business rules (negative amount, excessive value).
steps: Enter negative, zero, or excessively large values in numeric fields.
Test date/amount values outside the expected range.
Confirm server-side validation is consistent with client-side validation.
Assess the financial/functional impact of any logical inconsistencies.
tests.example: POST /cart/add  {"quantity":-5,"price":100}  # attempt to increase balance with a negative quantity

tests.title: Test Ability to Forge Requests
tests.description: Test that transactions are designed to be unpredictable/non-forgeable.
steps: Confirm authentication is mandatory for requests performed on behalf of a user.
Look for cases where transaction parameters (price, user ID) come from the client.
Confirm the server calculates critical values on its own side.
Test that values sent by the client are re-validated on the server.
tests.example: POST /checkout  {"productId":5,"price":0.01}  # changing the price sent from the client

tests.title: Test Integrity Checks
tests.description: Test that data integrity (signature, hash) is preserved across multi-step processes.
steps: Test whether data carried between steps (cart total, signature) can be modified.
If signature/hash validation exists, confirm it's enforced server-side.
Try bypassing the integrity check by skipping a step (jumping straight to the final step).
Document the financial impact of any weaknesses found.
tests.example: Modify the hidden 'total' field at the payment step and test whether the server notices

tests.title: Test for Process Timing
tests.description: Test whether time-based business rules (campaign duration, offer validity) can be bypassed.
steps: Check that time-limited transactions (flash sale, auction) are validated against server time.
Test whether a client-side time value can be manipulated.
Test whether a time limit can be bypassed via a race condition.
Confirm timestamp validation comes from a trusted source.
tests.example: Send the campaign-end request simultaneously multiple times to test for a race condition

tests.title: Test Number of Times a Function Can Be Used Limits
tests.description: Test whether limited-use functions, such as coupon redemption or trial attempts, can be reused.
steps: Try using a single-use function (coupon, invite code) more than once.
Try exceeding the limit by sending multiple concurrent requests via a race condition.
Try repeatedly triggering the same restriction with different accounts/sessions.
Confirm the limit is checked atomically on the server side.
tests.example: Try using the same coupon code in 50 concurrent requests with Turbo Intruder

tests.title: Testing for the Circumvention of Work Flows
tests.description: Test whether a multi-step process can be completed by skipping intermediate steps.
steps: Capture the request for each step of the process separately.
Try skipping intermediate steps and sending a request directly to the final step.
Test the behavior of changing the step order (step 3 before step 2).
Confirm the server validates step order (state-machine check).
tests.example: Skip the confirmation step and send a direct POST /order/complete request

tests.title: Test Defenses Against Application Misuse
tests.description: Test the adequacy of defenses against automated/bulk misuse (scraping, bots).
steps: Test that rate limiting is active on critical endpoints.
Assess whether CAPTCHA/bot-protection mechanisms can be bypassed.
Simulate a resource-consumption attack with bulk requests.
Check for the presence of IP/account-based anomaly detection.
tests.example: Send 100+ requests per second to the same endpoint and observe the rate-limit response

tests.title: Test Upload of Unexpected File Types
tests.description: Test whether the file-upload function accepts unexpected/dangerous file types.
steps: Try uploading disallowed extensions (.exe, .php).
Test whether the extension check is only enforced client-side.
Try bypassing the filter by altering the MIME type and file signature (magic bytes).
Try bypass techniques such as a double extension (.jpg.php).

tests.title: Test Upload of Malicious Files
tests.description: Test whether an uploaded file can be executed on the server side (RCE).
steps: Check whether the upload directory is directly reachable over the web.
Upload a file containing a web shell and test whether it's executable.
Try writing to a different directory by injecting path traversal into the file name.
Check whether uploaded files pass through an antivirus/sandbox scan.
tests.example: Upload shell.php and try reaching it with GET /uploads/shell.php?cmd=id

categories.name: Client-side Testing
categories.description: Test security flaws in code that runs in the browser (JavaScript, DOM).

tests.title: Testing for DOM-Based Cross Site Scripting
tests.description: Test cases where user input is processed directly through the DOM (location.hash, document.write) without going to the server, executing a script.
steps: Look for dangerous sinks such as innerHTML, document.write, or eval in the JS source code.
Trace whether the URL fragment (#) or query parameters reach these sinks.
Test whether different payload variations execute in the DOM.
Document the source-to-sink chain.

tests.title: Testing for JavaScript Execution
tests.description: Test whether user input reaches eval() or similar dynamic code-execution functions.
steps: Search the source code for uses of eval, Function(), or setTimeout(string).
If user input reaches these functions, inject a payload.
Test manipulation of the callback parameter on JSONP endpoints.
Document any executable code paths found.

tests.title: Testing for HTML Injection
tests.description: Test whether user input is interpreted as HTML, breaking the page structure.
steps: Send basic HTML tags (<h1>, <iframe>) into input fields.
Check whether the tag is rendered without being encoded in the response.
Try injecting a fake login form (phishing).
Document the impact with a screenshot.

tests.title: Testing for Client-side URL Redirect
tests.description: Test whether an open-redirect flaw can be used for phishing.
steps: Give the redirect parameter an external URL (?redirect=https://evil.com).
Try variations such as a relative path or a protocol-based bypass (//evil.com).
Confirm whether the redirect runs without a whitelist check.
Repeat the same test on OAuth/SSO flows (more critical impact).

tests.title: Testing for CSS Injection
tests.description: Test whether user-controlled CSS can be used to exfiltrate data from the page (attribute selector).
steps: Check whether user input reaches a style/CSS context.
Try an attribute-selector-based data-exfiltration payload (CSS keylogger).
Test whether sensitive values such as a CSRF token can be exfiltrated via CSS.
Check whether Content-Security-Policy prevents this.

tests.title: Testing for Client-side Resource Manipulation
tests.description: Test whether client-side business logic (price, permission checks) can be manipulated via JS/DOM.
steps: Check whether critical decisions (price calculation, form validation) are performed only in JS.
Test the impact of changing JS variables/the DOM live via DevTools.
Test whether disabled form fields are still processed server-side.
Document the points where server-side validation is missing.

tests.title: Testing Cross Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)
tests.description: Test whether the CORS configuration is overly permissive (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *).
steps: Change the Origin header to a random domain and check the response.
Check whether a wildcard/reflected origin is combined with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true.
Test whether a null origin or a subdomain wildcard is accepted.
Demonstrate with a PoC whether cross-origin reads from sensitive endpoints are possible.
tests.example:
curl -H "Origin: https://evil.com" -I https://target.com/api/user
# vulnerable if it returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://evil.com

tests.title: Testing for Cross Site Flashing
tests.description: Test whether Flash-based components (if any) are vulnerable to parameter injection.
steps: Check whether the application still uses .swf files.
Decompile the SWF file and look for ActionScript security flaws.
Test whether FlashVars parameters are vulnerable to injection.
Note that risk is low in modern browsers since Flash is no longer supported; state the currency of the finding.
tests.example: Analyze the .swf file with JPEXS Decompiler

tests.title: Testing for Clickjacking
tests.description: Test whether the page can be embedded in a transparent iframe to hijack user clicks.
steps: Check for the presence of the X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors headers.
Try loading the page as an iframe within a test HTML file.
Design a PoC targeting critical actions (account deletion, money transfer).
If no protection exists, document the impact with a screenshot.

tests.title: Testing WebSockets
tests.description: Test the security of WebSocket connections in terms of authentication, authorization and input validation.
steps: Check whether Origin validation is performed during the WebSocket handshake request.
Send injection payloads in messages sent over the connection.
Test that authentication is checked on every message, not just at connection time.
Confirm that wss:// (encrypted) is used.
tests.example: Capture and modify a message from the Burp Suite WebSockets History tab

tests.title: Testing Web Messaging
tests.description: Test whether postMessage() API usage accepts messages without origin validation.
steps: Search the JS source code for addEventListener('message', ...) usages.
Confirm whether the event.origin check is performed.
Test the impact of sending a forged postMessage from a different origin.
Check whether the message content is written unsafely into the DOM (turning into XSS).

tests.title: Testing Browser Storage
tests.description: Test whether sensitive data is kept unencrypted in localStorage/sessionStorage/IndexedDB.
steps: Review the stored data in the DevTools > Application tab.
Check whether a token, password, or personal data is stored in plaintext.
Assess whether this data could be stolen via XSS.
Note that sensitive data should only be kept in an HttpOnly cookie.
tests.example: Review the DevTools > Application > Local Storage tab

tests.title: Testing for Cross Site Script Inclusion
tests.description: Test whether JSON/JS-sourced data can be read by another origin via <script src> (JSONP/data leakage).
steps: Test whether authenticated JSON endpoints can be included with a <script> tag.
Check whether the JSONP callback parameter is restricted.
Assess whether array/object-formatted sensitive data can be read as a script.
Combine with CSRF to build a data-leakage PoC.

categories.name: API Testing
categories.description: Test security flaws specific to REST/GraphQL APIs.

tests.title: Testing GraphQL
tests.description: Test a GraphQL endpoint for introspection, excessive data querying, and authorization flaws.
steps: Send an introspection query and check whether the schema is exposed.
Test the DoS potential of deep/nested queries.
Test whether field-level authorization is applied consistently.
Try bypassing rate limits using batching.
